claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure containing an fcc matrix and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase.
The fcc matrix in the dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy is ferromagnetic.
The FeCoNiTi alloy exhibits magnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Changing the C14 phase fraction and local Ti concentration at fcc/C14 interfaces will modulate the interfacial magnetic exchange interaction.
At 400 K, thermal energy can overcome minor anisotropy barriers without fully decoupling the proposed antiferromagnetic exchange between the phases.
The fcc/C14 boundary acts as a magnetic exchange spring.
Ti 3d orbitals in the C14 phase mediate antiferromagnetic exchange with Fe, Co, and Ni 3d orbitals in the fcc phase.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at approximately 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient.
The Ti-rich C14 phase possesses a magnetic moment that couples antiferromagnetically to the fcc matrix.
Antiferromagnetic interaction with the secondary phase reduces the composite's net saturation magnetization.
The proposed interphase coupling increases magnetic anisotropy energy density.
Antiferromagnetically coupled fcc/C14 interfaces form rigid domain-wall pinning centers that impede magnetic reversal.
A magnetic contribution associated with an antiferromagnetic constituent can coincide with reduced saturation magnetization and increased coercivity in a 3d-transition-metal high-entropy alloy.
The interfacial pinning mechanism raises the coercivity of dual-phase FeCoNiTi to approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a pure fcc reference.
The fcc phase adjacent to C14 will exhibit spin-polarized density of states at the Fermi level and a distinct exchange-splitting shift.
Laves phases can form reticulated structures in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed coercivity mechanism requires the C14 phase to be continuous or reticulated at fcc grain boundaries and may fail for isolated C14 particles or insufficient Ti.
Spin-polarized DFT calculations comparing an isolated fcc model with an explicit fcc/C14 interface model can test the predicted Fermi-level density of states and exchange splitting.
Comparing C14-rich, dual-phase, and C14-suppressed FeCoNiTi specimens at 400 K can isolate whether the C14 phase is responsible for enhanced coercivity and reduced saturation magnetization.
